title: Streaming networking benchmarks: http vs grpc, chunking, proxies & backpressure
content:
Goal:
- Measure networking/streaming overhead for typical inference traffic patterns and evaluate differences across HTTP (1.1 chunked / HTTP/2) and gRPC streaming. Understand impact of chunk size, proxy (Envoy/Nginx) buffering, and backpressure/flow-control interactions. Produce actionable recommendations for default runtime settings and proxy configs.

Background / motivation:
- Serving runtime performance is sensitive to per-chunk overhead when responses are streamed token-by-token or in small micro-chunks (e.g., 16-128 bytes).
- Customers use a mix of direct-hosted API and deployments behind proxies/load-balancers; proxies can add latency and change flow-control semantics.
- We need to pick reasonable defaults (chunk size, keepalive, window sizes) and document proxy guidance to avoid regressions.

Testbed (hardware & infra) - baseline config:
- Model server: dedicated c6g.8xlarge-like instance (64 vCPU), 256 GB RAM, g4dn.12xlarge-equivalent GPU for heavy runs (tests repeated with/without GPU).
- Network: 10 Gbps host NIC, isolated subnet. All tests done with localhost (no hypervisor noise) and across two hosts for proxy scenarios.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.37 (optimizations branch), compiled with debug symbols off.
- TLS: tests run without TLS (to isolate pure networking overhead); a small set repeated with TLS enabled (see TODO).
- Clients: wrk2, ghz (gRPC), python aiohttp streaming client, and a simple Go gRPC streaming client.
- Proxies tested: Envoy (v1.25), Nginx (1.24), HAProxy (2.6) with default and tuned configs.

Workloads / patterns:
- Token-streaming: server emits small payloads frequently to simulate token-by-token generation. We varied per-chunk payload sizes: 128 B, 512 B, 1 KB, 4 KB, 16 KB, 64 KB.
- Batch-response streaming: server emits ~1 KB chunks at higher throughput.
- Long-lived connections: sustained streams for 30s to observe memory growth and flow control.
- Concurrency: single-connection high-throughput, and multi-connection (100, 200, 500 concurrent connections).

What we measured:
- p50/p95/p99 latency for token emission (time between request and first token, and between subsequent tokens)
- end-to-end throughput (tokens/sec)
- CPU usage (server and proxy), memory (RSS), and socket counts
- network stack metrics: packets/sec, retransmits (negligible on isolated testbed)
- backpressure events: server send-block times, client read stalls

Methodology notes / pitfalls:
- Avoiding client-side batching: some clients (curl, some SDKs) will buffer. We used explicit streaming libraries and small write-flush loops to simulate real SDK behavior.
- Measuring inter-token latency: instrumented server to emit timestamps per chunk to separate server processing time vs transport overhead.
- Proxy TCP buffers can hide backpressure in short runs; longer runs needed to surface memory growth.

Key results (summary):
1) HTTP/1.1 chunked vs HTTP/2 vs gRPC streaming:
   - gRPC (HTTP/2-based) shows lower per-chunk CPU overhead and better multiplexing under high concurrency. p99 inter-token latency ~0.6-1.1 ms lower than HTTP/1.1 chunked when chunk size <= 1 KB.
   - HTTP/2 unary+stream or gRPC streaming benefits from a single connection and flow-control windows; observed fewer socket churns and lower syscall rates.
   - HTTP/1.1 chunked has higher syscall and context-switch rates because proxies / servers often treat each chunk as a write->flush boundary.

2) Chunk size effects:
   - Very small chunks (<= 512 B): dramatically higher per-token CPU and syscalls. Throughput drops ~20-40% vs 4 KB chunks under same CPU.
   - 4 KB is a good knee: provides near-max throughput with acceptable latency. 1 KB performs slightly worse but is sometimes necessary for low-latency interactive scenarios.
   - Large chunks (>=16 KB): slightly higher latency for first token, but higher throughput for batched scenarios. Not suitable for sub-token streaming.

3) Proxies (Envoy/Nginx/HAProxy):
   - Default Envoy (with HTTP/2) introduces ~0.7-1.5 ms additional latency per token at small chunk sizes, mostly due to additional copy/buffer passes and thread-handoff when using filter chains. CPU overhead at proxy can be significant; observed proxy CPU at 10-30% of total in some configs.
   - Nginx (HTTP/1.1) with default configs shows head-of-line blocking for long-lived streams, and often buffers small writes into larger ones (good for throughput, bad for interactive immediacy).
   - HAProxy as TCP proxy had the lowest protocol-level overhead but lacked HTTP/2-aware features (unless configured), so multiplexing benefits lost.

4) Backpressure & flow-control:
   - Without proper flow control tuning (HTTP/2 window sizes, gRPC flow-control), server-side send buffers can grow under bursty traffic leading to memory bloat. We reproduced a pattern where GC pressure increased after a 2-minute burst.
   - gRPC/HTTP2 window tuning mitigates spikes: increasing initial window to 64 KB and stream window to 256 KB reduced transient server send-block times. However, overly large windows can delay detection of slow clients leading to memory use.

Representative numbers (server w/ gRPC vs HTTP/1.1 chunked, 100 concurrent streams, 1 KB chunks):
- gRPC: throughput ~120k tokens/s, p99 inter-token latency 2.1 ms, server CPU 65%
- HTTP/1.1 chunked: throughput ~95k tokens/s, p99 inter-token latency 3.2 ms, server CPU 78%
- Envoy (gRPC passthrough): throughput ~105k tokens/s, p99 inter-token latency 3.0 ms, envoy CPU 18%, server CPU 55%
(These are indicative; see raw csv files linked in Confluence page.)

Observations / deeper dives:
- syscall rate is the dominant cost in small-chunk streaming. Combining small writes into a single write or using splice-like zero-copy paths helps but requires changes in SDK/server.
- Event-loop vs thread-per-connection: our async runtime benefited at high concurrency; thread-per-connection led to more context-switch overhead for small chunks.
- Proxy filter chains: filters that inspect or mutate payloads (e.g., compression, auth) increase per-chunk latency substantially. Where possible, push those filters to the edge or avoid per-token processing.

Recommendations (actionable):
1) Default chunk size: adopt 4 KB as runtime recommended default chunk flush size for streaming responses. SDKs can offer 1 KB mode for extremely latency-sensitive usage, with caveats.
2) Prefer gRPC/HTTP2 for high-concurrency streaming: better multiplexing and lower syscall overhead.
3) Proxy guidance:
   - Use Envoy with HTTP/2 enabled and tuned thread-pools. Disable per-chunk buffering and reduce filter chain complexity on the hot path.
   - Avoid HTTP/1.1 proxies in front of token-streaming endpoints; if unavoidable, ensure proxy is configured to disable buffering and flush small chunks promptly.
4) Flow-control defaults: set HTTP/2 initial window = 64 KB and stream window = 256 KB as a balanced default. Instrument memory and add alarms for send-buffer growth.
5) SDK changes: provide batching layer that accumulates up to 4 KB before flush when using default settings; allow opt-out for ultra-low latency.
6) CI/benchmarks: add these streaming scenarios to the perf harness and track p99 inter-token latency and proxy CPU split in dashboards.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Run full matrix with TLS (TLS handshake and AES-NI overhead) and mTLS enforced (proxy + server).
- Re-run with real internet-like conditions (latency, packet loss) to measure retransmit/impact on flow-control dynamics.
- Evaluate zero-copy options (splice/sendfile) for within-host proxying where possible.
- Validate recommendations with Dedicated/Private deployments (different kernel/network stack).

Commands & quick reproducer notes:
- gRPC load (ghz): ghz --proto streaming.proto --call StreamingService.Stream --concurrency 100 --connections 10 --data "{\"prompt\":\"short\"}" --insecure --rps 0 --duration 30s
- HTTP streaming (wrk-like): custom wrk2 script that opens persistent connection and sends request then reads chunked responses; use lua script to measure inter-chunk times.
- Simple server instrumentation: log hex(chunk_size), timestamp_ns at emit. Use circular buffer to avoid I/O slowdowns while measuring.

Attachments & raw data:
- Raw CSVs and perf graphs uploaded to Confluence (see linked artifact). Benchmark scripts in GH-PR above.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc, early-ish; numbers vary by instance type and model workload. Focus on trends rather than absolute numbers.
- Please review the flow-control tuning recommendation and flag any security/compat concerns (e.g., window sizes + DoS surface).

Next steps:
- Add TLS runs and rerun Envoy with TLS termination (expected +0.5-1.0 ms additional latency).
- Add benchmarks for client SDK defaults (python/js/go) to see real-world flushing behavior.
- Draft an engineering RFC to standardize SDK/server defaults and Envoy configuration snippets.
